title: Man. Post. Cap. II §XIV: Placeus — bile reply; distinction not false; light vs darkness
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. I am not far from believing that this distinction of the first sin of Adam moved the bile of the Learned Man: so much does he attack and harass it from every side. But what does he set out to prove? that it was not necessary. Grant that it is so; provided it is not false, is not absurd, is not injurious to my cause, I do not see a cause why it ought to be so greatly agitated. But it distinguishes and disturbs the Reader. It distinguishes perhaps, but not for long. But it disturbs no one, unless if someone should wish me condemned and confuted. Light distinguishes and refreshes: darkness confounds and troubles. Moreover I deny that that distinction was not necessary. For so, the subject and attribute of the question having been distinguished, the labor of those who with so great effort oppose my opinion becomes vain: which seems to be the cause why these distinctions have been so greatly displeasing to them. But, he says, each one by himself can easily understand, since there were many sins of Adam, that inquiry is made concerning that one which among all was first. Therefore I expressed that which each by himself can easily understand: a great crime indeed, and one that deserves great rebuke!
pass_b_english: Placeus: I am nearly sure this distinction of Adam's first sin stirred the learned man's bile: he attacks and worries it from every side. What does he mean to prove? That it was unnecessary. Grant that; so long as it is not false, not absurd, and not harmful to my cause, I see no reason why it should be so fiercely chased. "But it distinguishes and confuses the reader." It distinguishes, perhaps—but not for long. It confuses no one unless someone wants me condemned and refuted. Light distinguishes and refreshes; darkness confounds and unsettles. Besides, I deny that the distinction was unnecessary. Once subject and attribute of the question are distinguished, the labor of those who batter my view with such effort is wasted—which seems why these distinctions so greatly displeased them. "But," he says, "anyone can easily see for himself that, though Adam had many sins, the question concerns the one that was first among them." So I stated what anyone can easily see for himself: a grave crime indeed, and one that deserves sharp rebuke!
source_text: PLAC. Parum abest quin credam, hanc primi peccati Adae distinctionem Viro Docto commovisse bilem: adeo eam omni ex parte adoritur & sollicitat. Quid autem probare instituit? illam non necessariam fuisse. Fac ita esse; modo non sit falsa, non sit absurda, non sit causae meae noxia, causam non video, cur tantopere debeat exagitari. At distinguit & obturbat Lectorem. Distinguit forte, sed non diu. Obturbat autem neminem, nisi si quis me damnatum velit & confutatum. Lux distinguit & recreat: tenebrae confundunt & turbant. Praeterea nego non fuisse necessariam illam distinctionem. Ita enim distinctis subjecto & attributo quaestionis irritus fit eorum labor, qui meam sententiam tanto molimine oppugnant: quae causa videtur esse, cur hae distinctiones eis tantopere ingratae fuerint. Sed, inquit, unusquisque per se facile intelligere potest, cum plura fuerint Adami peccata, de uno illo quaeri, quod inter omnia primum fuit. Ergo id expressi, quod quisque per se facile intelligere potest: Grande scilicet crimen, & quod magnam reprehensionem meretur!
